front: Why is a remote call fundamentally different from an in-process function call?
back: The caller cannot directly distinguish slow execution, message loss, network partition, or a crashed peer, and partial failure can leave uncertain state.
accepted_answers: The caller cannot directly distinguish slow execution, message loss, network partition, or a crashed peer, and partial failure can leave uncertain state.
hint: Latency and failure are independent across machines.

front: What is a partial failure?
back: Some components or communication links fail while the rest of the system continues running.
accepted_answers: Some components or communication links fail while the rest of the system continues running.
hint: The whole system does not fail together.

front: Why can a timeout never prove that the remote operation did not happen?
back: The request or response may have been delayed or lost after the server already committed the work.
accepted_answers: The request or response may have been delayed or lost after the server already committed the work.
hint: Silence is ambiguous.

front: What design requirement follows from retrying an operation after an ambiguous timeout?
back: The operation should be idempotent or deduplicated so repeating it cannot create an unintended second effect.
accepted_answers: The operation should be idempotent or deduplicated so repeating it cannot create an unintended second effect.
hint: The first attempt may have succeeded.

front: Why are distributed clocks difficult to use as a perfect global order?
back: Physical clocks drift, synchronization has error, and message delay means timestamps from different nodes may not reflect actual causality.
accepted_answers: Physical clocks drift, synchronization has error, and message delay means timestamps from different nodes may not reflect actual causality.
hint: Wall time is not a flawless order.

front: What does a logical clock capture?
back: A partial or total ordering of events based on communication and causality rather than exact wall-clock time.
accepted_answers: A partial or total ordering of events based on communication and causality rather than exact wall-clock time.
hint: Order events without claiming precise time.

front: What is the difference between concurrent events and causally related events?
back: Causally related events have an observable happens-before relationship; concurrent events have no known dependency ordering.
accepted_answers: Causally related events have an observable happens-before relationship; concurrent events have no known dependency ordering.
hint: Could one event have influenced the other?

front: Why can unbounded queues create cascading failure?
back: When arrival rate exceeds processing rate, queued work consumes memory and increases latency until timeouts, retries, and resource exhaustion spread pressure.
accepted_answers: When arrival rate exceeds processing rate, queued work consumes memory and increases latency until timeouts, retries, and resource exhaustion spread pressure.
hint: Backlog hides overload until it becomes worse.

front: How does backpressure reduce cascading failure?
back: It makes overload visible upstream so producers slow down, reject work, or shed load instead of creating an unlimited backlog.
accepted_answers: It makes overload visible upstream so producers slow down, reject work, or shed load instead of creating an unlimited backlog.
hint: Control admission before resources collapse.

front: Why can retries amplify an outage?
back: Failed or slow requests generate extra attempts, increasing load on the already unhealthy dependency and delaying recovery.
accepted_answers: Failed or slow requests generate extra attempts, increasing load on the already unhealthy dependency and delaying recovery.
hint: More traffic is sent when capacity is lowest.

front: What is a crash-stop failure model?
back: A failed process halts and never returns during the modeled execution.
accepted_answers: A failed process halts and never returns during the modeled execution.
hint: Failure is permanent for the run.

front: What is a crash-recovery failure model?
back: A process may stop and later restart, retaining only state that was persisted durably.
accepted_answers: A process may stop and later restart, retaining only state that was persisted durably.
hint: Recovery changes what memory survives.

front: What is an omission fault?
back: A process or link fails to send, receive, or deliver one or more messages.
accepted_answers: A process or link fails to send, receive, or deliver one or more messages.
hint: Expected communication is missing.

front: What is an arbitrary or Byzantine fault?
back: A component can behave inconsistently or maliciously, including sending conflicting information to different peers.
accepted_answers: A component can behave inconsistently or maliciously, including sending conflicting information to different peers.
hint: The failure is not limited to silence.

front: What lesson does the Two Generals problem provide?
back: Over an unreliable channel, finite message exchanges cannot create absolute common knowledge that both parties will act.
accepted_answers: Over an unreliable channel, finite message exchanges cannot create absolute common knowledge that both parties will act.
hint: Acknowledgments can also be lost.

front: What does the FLP result imply for asynchronous consensus?
back: With even one possible crash, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination in every fully asynchronous execution.
accepted_answers: With even one possible crash, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination in every fully asynchronous execution.
hint: Safety may hold while progress can be delayed forever.

front: How do practical systems make progress despite FLP?
back: They assume periods of synchrony, use timeouts and randomized or leader-based mechanisms, and guarantee liveness only when timing conditions improve.
accepted_answers: They assume periods of synchrony, use timeouts and randomized or leader-based mechanisms, and guarantee liveness only when timing conditions improve.
hint: Real systems weaken the model.

front: What is a failure detector?
back: A mechanism that produces suspicions about whether remote processes are alive.
accepted_answers: A mechanism that produces suspicions about whether remote processes are alive.
hint: It estimates failure; it does not observe it directly.

front: Why are heartbeat timeouts a trade-off rather than a perfect threshold?
back: Short timeouts detect failures quickly but create more false suspicions; long timeouts reduce false positives but delay recovery.
accepted_answers: Short timeouts detect failures quickly but create more false suspicions; long timeouts reduce false positives but delay recovery.
hint: Speed versus accuracy.

front: What does a phi-accrual failure detector output?
back: A continuously increasing suspicion level derived from recent heartbeat arrival statistics rather than a fixed alive/dead verdict.
accepted_answers: A continuously increasing suspicion level derived from recent heartbeat arrival statistics rather than a fixed alive/dead verdict.
hint: The consumer chooses the threshold.

front: Why can outsourcing heartbeats improve failure detection?
back: A separate observer may remain responsive when the application process is overloaded and can distinguish service saturation from total host failure.
accepted_answers: A separate observer may remain responsive when the application process is overloaded and can distinguish service saturation from total host failure.
hint: Do not make an unhealthy worker judge itself.

front: What problem does leader election solve?
back: It selects one participant to coordinate work that requires a single temporary authority.
accepted_answers: It selects one participant to coordinate work that requires a single temporary authority.
hint: Choose one coordinator among peers.

front: Why must a newly elected leader prove it is current before accepting writes?
back: An old or stale leader may not contain the latest committed state and could overwrite newer decisions or create split-brain behavior.
accepted_answers: An old or stale leader may not contain the latest committed state and could overwrite newer decisions or create split-brain behavior.
hint: Leadership requires an epoch or term, not just a name.

front: What is split brain?
back: Multiple nodes simultaneously believe they are the authoritative leader and accept conflicting operations.
accepted_answers: Multiple nodes simultaneously believe they are the authoritative leader and accept conflicting operations.
hint: Two authorities act on one logical system.

front: How do fencing tokens help prevent stale leaders from corrupting state?
back: Each leadership term receives a monotonically increasing token, and downstream resources reject operations carrying an older token.
accepted_answers: Each leadership term receives a monotonically increasing token, and downstream resources reject operations carrying an older token.
hint: Authority must be checked at the protected resource.

front: What is CAP actually concerned with during a network partition?
back: A replicated system must choose whether to preserve a single consistent view or keep every partition available for operations that may diverge.
accepted_answers: A replicated system must choose whether to preserve a single consistent view or keep every partition available for operations that may diverge.
hint: The trade-off is forced only when communication is broken.

front: Why is 'choose two of three' an oversimplification of CAP?
back: Partition tolerance is not a normal on/off feature in a distributed system, and systems make operation-specific, time-dependent trade-offs beyond one fixed label.
accepted_answers: Partition tolerance is not a normal on/off feature in a distributed system, and systems make operation-specific, time-dependent trade-offs beyond one fixed label.
hint: The model applies under partition.

front: What is linearizability?
back: Each operation appears to take effect atomically between its invocation and response, respecting real-time order.
accepted_answers: Each operation appears to take effect atomically between its invocation and response, respecting real-time order.
hint: A single-copy illusion with real-time constraints.

front: How does sequential consistency differ from linearizability?
back: All operations follow one common order consistent with each client's program order, but that order need not respect real-time completion.
accepted_answers: All operations follow one common order consistent with each client's program order, but that order need not respect real-time completion.
hint: Global order without the real-time rule.

front: What is causal consistency?
back: Operations that may have influenced one another are observed in causal order, while concurrent operations may be seen in different orders.
accepted_answers: Operations that may have influenced one another are observed in causal order, while concurrent operations may be seen in different orders.
hint: Preserve dependencies, allow concurrency.

front: What does eventual consistency guarantee when updates stop?
back: Replicas will converge to the same state after sufficient communication and reconciliation.
accepted_answers: Replicas will converge to the same state after sufficient communication and reconciliation.
hint: No new writes, enough time.

front: Why is eventual consistency alone insufficient as an application contract?
back: It does not specify how stale reads may be, how conflicts resolve, or what ordering a client observes during convergence.
accepted_answers: It does not specify how stale reads may be, how conflicts resolve, or what ordering a client observes during convergence.
hint: Convergence leaves many user-visible behaviors undefined.

front: What is read-your-writes consistency?
back: A client session will not read a state older than its own successful writes.
accepted_answers: A client session will not read a state older than its own successful writes.
hint: Your next read includes what you just saved.

front: What are monotonic reads?
back: Once a session observes a version, later reads in that session do not return an older version.
accepted_answers: Once a session observes a version, later reads in that session do not return an older version.
hint: A client's view never moves backward.

front: What are monotonic writes?
back: Writes from one session are applied in the order the session issued them.
accepted_answers: Writes from one session are applied in the order the session issued them.
hint: Preserve client write order.

front: Why can sticky sessions help provide client-centric guarantees?
back: Routing a client to the same sufficiently current replica makes it easier to preserve session history, though failover must transfer or reconstruct that context.
accepted_answers: Routing a client to the same sufficiently current replica makes it easier to preserve session history, though failover must transfer or reconstruct that context.
hint: Keep the user on one consistent view.

front: What is tunable consistency?
back: The client or operation chooses read and write quorum levels, trading latency and availability against freshness and overlap guarantees.
accepted_answers: The client or operation chooses read and write quorum levels, trading latency and availability against freshness and overlap guarantees.
hint: Consistency can be selected per operation.

front: Why does quorum overlap matter?
back: If read and write quorums intersect, at least one replica consulted by a read should contain the latest successful write under the model's assumptions.
accepted_answers: If read and write quorums intersect, at least one replica consulted by a read should contain the latest successful write under the model's assumptions.
hint: The sets share a member.

front: Why can a quorum read still return stale data in a poorly designed system?
back: Replica versions may be incomparable, clocks may be unsafe, membership may change, or the resolver may choose incorrectly; quorum size alone is not a complete protocol.
accepted_answers: Replica versions may be incomparable, clocks may be unsafe, membership may change, or the resolver may choose incorrectly; quorum size alone is not a complete protocol.
hint: Numbers need versioning and reconciliation semantics.

front: What makes a CRDT useful in an eventually consistent system?
back: Its updates or states merge deterministically so replicas converge without central coordination when all changes are delivered.
accepted_answers: Its updates or states merge deterministically so replicas converge without central coordination when all changes are delivered.
hint: The data type embeds conflict resolution.
